hints: Look past the words equal masses and focus on the building blocks. What single type of monomer makes up both amylose and amylopectin?
Remember that both amylose and amylopectin are starch polysaccharides joined by alpha 1,4 and alpha 1,6 glycosidic bonds, so complete hydrolysis will release only that same alpha monomer.
walkthrough:
**Recall what amylose and amylopectin are**

Both are polysaccharides of starch found in plants. Amylose is unbranched, amylopectin is branched, but that is only a difference in shape.

Key point: both are polymers of $\alpha$-glucose only.

**Apply what complete hydrolysis means**

Hydrolysis breaks every glycosidic bond by adding water. Complete hydrolysis means every bond is broken, so the polymer is cut right back to its monomers.

Rule: polymer of $\alpha$-glucose + water gives $\alpha$-glucose monomers.

**Conclude the products**

Since you started with only $\alpha$-glucose chains, you can only finish with $\alpha$-glucose. The equal masses detail does not create a new product, it just means you get a large amount of the same monomer.

options.A: Correct. Both amylose and amylopectin are made entirely from alpha-glucose, so complete hydrolysis releases alpha-glucose only.
options.B: Not correct. Beta-glucose is the monomer of cellulose, not of starch. Neither amylose nor amylopectin contains beta-glucose.
options.C: Not correct. Equal starting masses do not mean two different products. Both starting molecules give the same single product.
options.D: Not correct. This suggests some beta-glucose is made alongside more alpha-glucose, but zero beta-glucose is produced at all.
